## Introduction

This page contains optional self-study material that builds on the
[w4c lecture](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd),
where you learned the basics of `grep`, `cut`, `sort`, and `uniq`.
Here, you'll go further with those commands and learn several new ones:

- [Regular expressions](#regular-expressions-with-grep),
  to search for text _patterns_ rather than fixed text
- [More `sort` and `uniq`](#more-sort-and-uniq-and-friends),
  plus the related commands `column`, `paste`, and `comm`
- [`tr`](#tr-to-translate-characters) to substitute or delete single characters
- [`awk`](#awk-for-tabular-data-processing) to filter and process tabular data
- [`sed`](#sed-to-find-and-replace) to find and replace text, and more
- [`join`](#putting-it-together-genes-per-chromosome) to merge two tables,
  in a final example that combines many of these tools

Throughout, you'll work with the files from the @garrigós2025 dataset,
plus the _Culex pipiens_ genome assembly FASTA file.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Aim for reading fluency, not memorization
`awk` and `sed` are small programming languages in their own right,
and nobody remembers all of their syntax.
Aim to understand what the examples do,
so that you can recognize, adapt, and look up such commands later.
This also matters for week 8: generative AI is quite good at writing one-liners
like the ones on this page, but you'll need to be able to read them
to check that they do what you want.
:::

### Setting up

1. At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>, start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.

2. Create a dir for this page and move into it:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p week04/data-tools
   cd week04/data-tools
   ```

3. Copy the metadata file and one FASTQ file, like in w4c:

   ```bash
   cp ../../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv .
   cp ../../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz .
   ```

4. Create a decompressed copy of the GTF file.
   This way, you won't have to start every command with `zcat`:

   ```bash
   zcat ../../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz > annot.gtf
   ```

5. Download the genome assembly FASTA file from NCBI with `wget`,
   create a decompressed copy named `genome.fna`, and remove the compressed file:

   ```bash
   wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/016/801/865/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2/GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
   zcat GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz > genome.fna
   rm GCF_016801865.2_TS_CPP_V2_genomic.fna.gz
   ```

   ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
   `wget` downloads a file from a URL.
   You'll learn more about it, and download this same file again,
   in week 10.
   :::

6. Check that you have these four files:

   ```bash
   ls -lh
   ```
   ```bash-out
   -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 123M Sep 21 10:12 annot.gtf
   -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 547M Sep 21 10:13 genome.fna
   -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471  457 Sep 21 10:11 metadata.tsv
   -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471  21M Sep 21 10:11 S63_R1.fastq.gz
   ```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
The decompressed genome FASTA takes up quite a bit of space,
so remove `genome.fna` once you're done with this page.
:::

## Regular expressions with `grep`

### What are regular expressions?

In w4c, you used `grep` to search for fixed text, like `relictum`.
But `grep` actually interprets its search pattern as a **regular expression** ("regex"):
a pattern in which some characters have a special meaning.
With regular expressions, you can for example search for:

- Lines that _start_ with a `>` (the header lines of a FASTA file)
- Reads that end in a stretch of 15 or more `A`s
- Any text between quotes that follows `gene_id` in a GTF file

Regular expressions are used far beyond `grep`:
`sed` and `awk` (later on this page) use them,
as do R and Python, and even VS Code's search box
(click the `.*` button in the search box to turn on regex search).
So, time spent learning them pays off in many places.

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Use single quotes around regular expressions
Some regex symbols, like `$` and `\`, also have a special meaning to the shell.
Inside double quotes, the shell may therefore change the pattern
before `grep` gets to see it.
Inside **single quotes**, the shell leaves everything alone,
so on this page, we'll use single quotes around regular expressions.
:::

### Anchors: `^` and `$`

By default, a pattern can match anywhere in a line.
**`^`** anchors a pattern to the **start** of a line,
and **`$`** anchors it to the **end** of a line.
To see the difference, search the sample IDs in the metadata file
(column 1) for the number `6`:

```bash
cut -f 1 metadata.tsv | grep '6'
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>S7<span class="match-red">6</span>
S8<span class="match-red">6</span>
S<span class="match-red">6</span>4
S<span class="match-red">6</span>7
S<span class="match-red">66</span>
S<span class="match-red">6</span>9
S<span class="match-red">6</span>3
S<span class="match-red">6</span>5
S<span class="match-red">6</span>8</code></pre>

```bash
# Only sample IDs that start with 'S6':
cut -f 1 metadata.tsv | grep '^S6'
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="match-red">S6</span>4
<span class="match-red">S6</span>7
<span class="match-red">S6</span>6
<span class="match-red">S6</span>9
<span class="match-red">S6</span>3
<span class="match-red">S6</span>5
<span class="match-red">S6</span>8</code></pre>

```bash
# Only sample IDs that end with '6':
cut -f 1 metadata.tsv | grep '6$'
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>S7<span class="match-red">6</span>
S8<span class="match-red">6</span>
S6<span class="match-red">6</span></code></pre>

Anchors are especially useful with genomics files,
in which certain types of lines start with a specific character.
For example, to count the sequences in a FASTA file,
count its header lines, which start with a `>`:

```bash
grep -c '^>' genome.fna
```
```bash-out
290
```

Let's also look at the first few headers:

```bash
grep '^>' genome.fna | head -n 5
```
```bash-out
>NC_068937.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 1, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
>NC_068938.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 2, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
>NC_068939.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 3, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
>NW_026292818.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS unplaced genomic scaffold, TS_CPP_V2 Cpp_Un0001, whole genome shotgun sequence
>NW_026292819.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS unplaced genomic scaffold, TS_CPP_V2 Cpp_Un0002, whole genome shotgun sequence
```

So, the genome assembly consists of 290 sequences:
the three _Culex_ chromosomes, and many smaller "unplaced scaffolds"
(pieces of the genome that could not be assigned to a chromosome).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Combining both anchors, `^$` matches **empty lines**,
so `grep -v '^$'` removes all empty lines from its input.
:::

### Any character (`.`), repetition (`*`), and `grep -o`

Two more key regex symbols are:

- **`.`** --- matches any **single character**.
- **`*`** --- matches the **preceding character** any number of times, including zero.

Together, **`.*`** therefore matches any number of any characters,
like the `*` shell wildcard does.

To see exactly what a regular expression matches, use `grep`'s **`-o`** option,
which prints **only the matching part** of each line instead of the full line.
Let's try to extract the gene ID (the quoted text after `gene_id`)
from the first line of the GTF file's table part:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | head -n 1 | grep -o 'gene_id ".*"'
```
```bash-out
gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; description "homeotic protein deformed"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120427725"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"
```

That's a lot more than we wanted!
The problem is that `.*` is "**greedy**": it matches as much as possible,
so the match runs all the way to the _last_ `"` on the line.
Character classes, discussed next, offer a solution.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
To match one of these special characters literally,
put a backslash before it ("escape" it).
For example, `NC_068937\.1` only matches an actual period between `7` and `1`,
while `NC_068937.1` would also match, e.g., `NC_06893701`.
:::

### Character classes: `[...]` and `[^...]`

A **character class** matches **one character from a set**,
which you list between square brackets:

- `[ACGT]` matches a single `A`, `C`, `G`, _or_ `T`.
- Ranges are allowed: `[0-9]` matches any digit, and `[a-z]` any lowercase letter.
- A `^` as the _first_ character inside the brackets **negates** the class:
  `[^ACGT]` matches any single character that is _not_ `A`, `C`, `G`, or `T`.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Note the two different meanings of `^`:
_outside_ brackets, it anchors to the start of a line,
while as the first character _inside_ brackets, it negates the character class.
:::

Negated character classes are the solution to our greedy matching problem.
Instead of "any characters, followed by a quote" (`.*"`),
we ask for "any characters _except_ a quote, followed by a quote" (`[^"]*"`).
This way, the match can't extend beyond the next quote:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | head -n 1 | grep -o 'gene_id "[^"]*"'
```
```bash-out
gene_id "LOC120427725"
```

The same trick works to extract just the sequence IDs from the FASTA headers ---
everything after the `>` up until the first space:

```bash
grep -o '^>[^ ]*' genome.fna | head -n 4
```
```bash-out
>NC_068937.1
>NC_068938.1
>NC_068939.1
>NW_026292818.1
```

#### Extracting and counting matches

Combining `grep -o` with the `sort | uniq -c` frequency-table approach from w4c
is a very handy way to summarize information that is "hidden" inside a column.
For example, the GTF file's attribute column (column 9) has a `gene_biotype`
for every gene. How many genes of each type are there?

```bash
grep -o 'gene_biotype "[^"]*"' annot.gtf | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```
```bash-out
  16297 gene_biotype "protein_coding"
   1620 gene_biotype "lncRNA"
    842 gene_biotype "pseudogene"
    686 gene_biotype "tRNA"
    155 gene_biotype "rRNA"
     58 gene_biotype "snRNA"
      9 gene_biotype "snoRNA"
      5 gene_biotype "transcribed_pseudogene"
      1 gene_biotype "misc_RNA"
```

Most genes are protein-coding,
but the annotation also includes, e.g., about 1,600 long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes.

### Extended regular expressions: `grep -E`

Several other useful regex symbols are only available as
"**extended** regular expressions", which you can turn on with `grep -E`:

| Symbol    | Matches | Example | Example matches
|-----------|---------|---------|----------------
| `+`       | The preceding character **one or more** times | `[0-9]+` | `7`, `2046`
| `?`       | The preceding character **zero or one** time | `genes?` | `gene`, `genes`
| `{n}`     | The preceding character **exactly _n_** times | `A{3}` | `AAA`
| `{n,}`    | The preceding character **at least _n_** times | `A{3,}` | `AAA`, `AAAAAA`
| `{n,m}`   | The preceding character **_n_ to _m_** times | `A{3,5}` | `AAA`, `AAAAA`
| <code>&#124;</code> | **Either** the pattern on the left **or** the one on the right | <code>cecropin&#124;defensin</code> | `cecropin`, `defensin`
| `( )`     | **Groups** a pattern, e.g. to repeat it | `(CA)+` | `CA`, `CACACA`

: {.striped .hover}

For example, how many reads in the FASTQ file end in at least 15 `A`s,
which may be the poly-A tails of mRNAs?

```bash
zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | grep -cE 'A{15,}$'
```
```bash-out
199
```

And which GTF features belong to genes for the antimicrobial peptides
cecropin or defensin, which are part of the mosquito immune response?

```bash
grep -E 'cecropin|defensin' annot.gtf | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c
```
```bash-out
     16 CDS
     17 exon
      7 gene
      8 start_codon
      8 stop_codon
      8 transcript
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Basic vs. extended regular expressions _(Click to expand)_

Without `-E`, `grep` uses "**basic**" regular expressions,
in which `+`, `?`, `{ }`, `|`, and `( )` are just literal characters.
In the GNU version of `grep` (which is what OSC uses),
you can still use their special meaning by putting a backslash before them:

| Extended (`grep -E`) | Basic (`grep`) |
|----------------------|----------------|
| `A+`                 | `A\+`          |
| `A{15,}`             | `A\{15,\}`     |
| <code>cecropin&#124;defensin</code> | <code>cecropin\&#124;defensin</code> |

: {.striped .hover}

That gets hard to read quickly,
so it's easiest to simply use `-E` whenever you need these symbols.
The same goes for `sed`, which also has an `-E` option.
`awk` always uses extended regular expressions.

When searching online, you'll also come across
"Perl-compatible" regular expressions (`grep -P`),
which offer additional shortcuts.
For example, `\t` matches a Tab with `grep -P`, but not with `grep` or `grep -E`:

```bash
# Print lines with 'gene' as the feature type (column 3), surrounded by Tabs:
grep -P '\tgene\t' annot.gtf | head -n 2
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Printing full FASTQ records with `grep -A` and `-B` _(Click to expand)_

When you search a FASTQ file for a sequence,
`grep` only prints the matching sequence line.
To see the full 4-line FASTQ record of each matching read,
also print 1 line **b**efore (`-B 1`) and 2 lines **a**fter (`-A 2`) each match.
The `--no-group-separator` option prevents `grep` from printing `--` lines
between non-adjacent matches, so that the output is valid FASTQ:

```bash
zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | grep --no-group-separator -B 1 -A 2 -E 'A{15,}$' | head -n 8
```
```bash-out
@ERR10802863.17755922 17755922 length=73
AGAATGCATACACAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
+
AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
@ERR10802863.21692370 21692370 length=73
AGATCAACTACTGAGAAATGTGTTGAGCGATAAATACAGTTCATTAAAATCAACCAGAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
+
AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
```
:::

### Regular expressions vs. shell wildcards

Regular expressions and the shell wildcards from w4b
(and the [More Unix shell](shell.qmd#other-shell-wildcards) page)
look similar, but they are different things:

- **Shell wildcards** match **file names**,
  and are expanded by the shell _before_ a command runs.
- **Regular expressions** match **text** in a command's input,
  and are interpreted by the command itself (e.g. `grep`).

Confusingly, some symbols have a different meaning in each:

| Shell wildcard | Regex equivalent | Matches
|----------------|------------------|--------------------------
| `?`            | `.`              | Any single character
| `*`            | `.*`             | Any number of any characters
| `[...]` and `[^...]` | Same       | One character that is / is not in the set

: {.striped .hover}

Also recall from w4c that `grep` patterns don't need to match the entire line,
whereas a glob pattern has to match the entire file name.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: Regular expressions

a. Thinking of the shell wildcard `S6*`, a classmate expects the command below
   to count the 7 samples whose ID starts with `S6`.
   What count do you think it will report instead, and why?
   Run the command to check your answer.

   ```bash
   cut -f 1 metadata.tsv | grep -c 'S6*'
   ```

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   It reports `22`: every single sample ID.

   In a regular expression, `*` means "the preceding character any number of times,
   _including zero_".
   So, `S6*` matches an `S` followed by zero or more `6`s ---
   and every sample ID contains an `S`.

   The regex equivalent of the wildcard is `S6.*`,
   but since `grep` patterns don't need to match the full line,
   plain `S6` (or, more precisely, `^S6`) is all you need here.
   </details>

b. Count the number of FASTA headers that start with `>NC`,
   and the number that start with `>NW`, and print the `>NC` headers.
   What do the `NC` sequences represent, and what do the `NW` ones represent?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```bash
   grep -c '^>NC' genome.fna
   ```
   ```bash-out
   4
   ```
   ```bash
   grep -c '^>NW' genome.fna
   ```
   ```bash-out
   286
   ```
   ```bash
   grep '^>NC' genome.fna
   ```
   ```bash-out
   >NC_068937.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 1, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
   >NC_068938.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 2, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
   >NC_068939.1 Culex pipiens pallens isolate TS chromosome 3, TS_CPP_V2, whole genome shotgun sequence
   >NC_015079.1 Culex pipiens pipiens mitochondrion, complete genome
   ```

   The 4 `NC` sequences are the 3 chromosomes plus the mitochondrial genome,
   while the 286 `NW` sequences are the unplaced scaffolds
   (in NCBI's RefSeq database, `NC_` IDs are used for complete molecules
   like chromosomes, and `NW_` IDs for scaffolds).
   </details>

c. A labmate counts the reads in a FASTQ file by counting the header lines,
   which start with `@`:

   ```bash
   zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@'
   ```

   For this file, that gives the correct answer of 500,000 reads.
   But why could this approach overcount the reads in other FASTQ files?
   _(Hint: think about the quality scores, and see the table in the_
   _[w4a FASTQ quality score slides](../week04/w4a_genomics-files.qmd#fastq-quality-scores).)_

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   The `@` character is also used as a quality score:
   it represents a Phred score of 31 (one more than `?`, which represents 30).
   So, a quality score line can start with an `@`,
   and would then be counted as a read.

   It happens to work for our file because its quality scores are "binned"
   into just a few values, none of which is 31.
   More robust approaches are to divide the number of lines by 4,
   or to search for a longer, more specific header pattern like `'^@ERR'`.
   </details>

d. How many genes have a description that contains "heat shock",
   and are any of these descriptions shared by multiple genes?
   _(Hint: `description` attributes are only present on `gene` lines,_
   _so you can adapt the `gene_biotype` command above.)_

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Allow any characters except a quote both before and after "heat shock",
   so that the match stays within the description's quotes:

   ```bash
   grep -o 'description "[^"]*heat shock[^"]*"' annot.gtf | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
   ```
   ```bash-out
         3 description "heat shock protein 70 B2"
         2 description "heat shock 70 kDa protein cognate 4-like"
         1 description "heat shock protein beta-1"
         1 description "heat shock protein 83-like"
         1 description "heat shock protein 83"
         1 description "heat shock protein 75 kDa, mitochondrial"
         1 description "heat shock protein 70 A2-like"
         1 description "heat shock protein 60A-like"
         1 description "heat shock factor-binding protein 1"
         1 description "heat shock factor protein"
         1 description "heat shock 70 kDa protein cognate 5"
         1 description "heat shock 70 kDa protein cognate 4"
         1 description "heat shock 70 kDa protein cognate 2"
         1 description "heat shock 70 kDa protein 4"
         1 description "activator of 90 kDa heat shock protein ATPase homolog 1"
         1 description "10 kDa heat shock protein, mitochondrial"
   ```

   There are 16 distinct descriptions, two of which are shared by multiple genes.
   To count the genes, count the matching lines:

   ```bash
   grep -c 'description "[^"]*heat shock' annot.gtf
   ```
   ```bash-out
   19
   ```
   </details>
:::

## More `sort` and `uniq`, and friends

### Sorting by column, numerically

In w4c, you saw that `sort -k` sorts by specific columns,
and that `sort -n` sorts numerically.
You can combine the two by adding an `n` to a specific column (key).

To try this, create a small file with the sequence ID, feature type,
and start and end positions (columns 1 and 3-5) of the first 6 genes in the GTF file.
(The `-w` option makes `grep` only match `gene` as a whole word.)

```bash
cut -f 1,3-5 annot.gtf | grep -w 'gene' | head -n 6 > genes6.tsv
cat genes6.tsv
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     gene    2046    110808
NC_068937.1     gene    48457   50554
NC_068937.1     gene    76295   82374
NC_068937.1     gene    82671   86331
NC_068937.1     gene    160196  177583
NC_068937.1     gene    299209  303777
```

These genes are already sorted by their start position (column 3 in this file).
But see what happens when you sort them by that column
_without_ telling `sort` that it contains numbers:

```bash
sort -k3,3 genes6.tsv
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     gene    160196  177583
NC_068937.1     gene    2046    110808
NC_068937.1     gene    299209  303777
NC_068937.1     gene    48457   50554
NC_068937.1     gene    76295   82374
NC_068937.1     gene    82671   86331
```

Sorting alphabetically, `sort` compares character by character,
so `160196` comes before `2046` because `1` comes before `2`.
With `-k3,3n`, you get the correct numeric order back:

```bash
sort -k3,3n genes6.tsv
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     gene    2046    110808
NC_068937.1     gene    48457   50554
NC_068937.1     gene    76295   82374
NC_068937.1     gene    82671   86331
NC_068937.1     gene    160196  177583
NC_068937.1     gene    299209  303777
```

A common use of this is to sort an annotation file by position,
first by sequence ID (alphabetically) and then by start position (numerically).
For the GTF file, whose start positions are in column 4, that would be:

```bash
# [Example only, no need to run this]
sort -k1,1 -k4,4n annot.gtf
```

Many genomics tools require their input files to be sorted this way.

### Other useful `sort` options

- **`-c`** checks whether a file is already sorted.
  It prints nothing if the file is sorted, and reports the first out-of-order line if not:

  ```bash
  sort -c -k3,3n genes6.tsv
  ```
  ```bash
  sort -c -k3,3 genes6.tsv
  ```
  ```bash-out
  sort: genes6.tsv:5: disorder: NC_068937.1     gene    160196  177583
  ```

- **`-u`** only keeps unique lines, so `sort -u` does the same as `sort | uniq`.

- **`-V`** ("version sort") sorts numbers _within text_ by their numeric value:

  ```bash
  # printf prints text like echo does, and '\n' starts a new line:
  printf "sample1\nsample10\nsample2\n" | sort -V
  ```
  ```bash-out
  sample1
  sample2
  sample10
  ```

  _(Without `-V`, `sample10` would come before `sample2`.)_

- **`-g`** sorts numbers in scientific notation (like `1e-5`) correctly,
  which `-n` doesn't.
  This is useful for, e.g., p-values.

- **`-t`** sets the column delimiter, which by default is any whitespace.
  For example, `sort -t , -k2,2` sorts a CSV file by its second column.

### Finding duplicates with `uniq -d`

With the **`-d`** option, `uniq` only prints lines that occur more than once
(one copy of each).
For example, how many gene descriptions are shared by multiple genes?

```bash
grep -o 'description "[^"]*"' annot.gtf | sort | uniq -d | wc -l
```
```bash-out
1424
```

To see which descriptions are shared by the most genes,
use the frequency table approach instead:

```bash
grep -o 'description "[^"]*"' annot.gtf | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5
```
```bash-out
    156 description "5S ribosomal RNA"
    141 description "uncharacterized protein K02A2.6-like"
     44 description "pickpocket protein 28-like"
     41 description "transfer RNA valine (anticodon AAC)"
     39 description "transfer RNA tyrosine (anticodon GUA)"
```

_(The 156 5S ribosomal RNA genes are not an error:_
_rRNA genes typically occur in many copies in a genome.)_

### `column -t` for viewing tabular files

When the values in a column differ in length,
tabular files can look messy in the terminal:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | cut -f 1-8 | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  gene    2046    110808  .       +       .
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  transcript      2046    110808  .       +       .
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  exon    2046    2531    .       +       .
```

`column -t` lines up the columns nicely:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | cut -f 1-8 | head -n 3 | column -t
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1  Gnomon  gene        2046  110808  .  +  .
NC_068937.1  Gnomon  transcript  2046  110808  .  +  .
NC_068937.1  Gnomon  exon        2046  2531    .  +  .
```

`column` is only meant for viewing:
it separates columns with spaces, so don't save its output as a TSV file.
For a CSV file, specify the delimiter with `-s`: `column -s , -t my-data.csv`.

### `paste` to combine lines

`paste` combines lines **side by side**, separated by Tabs.
Given two files, it pastes line 1 of the first file next to line 1 of the second, and so on.

A neat trick is to give `paste` a dash (`-`) for each line it should combine
from its standard input.
With four dashes, `paste` combines every four lines into one ---
which turns each 4-line FASTQ record into a single line:

```bash
zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | paste - - - - | head -n 2
```
```bash-out
@ERR10802863.8435456 8435456 length=74  CAACGAATACATCATGTTTGCGAAACTACTCCTCCTCGCCTTGGTGGGGATCAGTACTGCGTACCAGTATGAGT      +       AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
@ERR10802863.27637245 27637245 length=74        GCCACACTTTTGAAGAACAGCGTCATTGTTCTTAATTTTGTCGGCAACGCCTGCACGAGCCTTCCACGTAAGTT      +       AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEAEE<EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
```

Now that each read is one line, with the sequence in column 2,
you can use all the column-based tools you know.
For example, which read sequences occur most often?

```bash
zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | paste - - - - | cut -f 2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5
```
```bash-out
  32589 NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
    255 ATAAATTAAAGGGCCGCAGTATTTTGACTGTGCGAAGGTAGCATAATCACTAGTCTTTTAATTGGAGGCTTGT
    223 AACAGCGTAATTTTTTTTTAGAGTTCATATCGACAAAAAAGATTGCGACCTCGATGTTGGATTAAGAGTTATTT
    204 AAATTAAAGGGCCGCAGTATTTTGACTGTGCGAAGGTAGCATAATCACTAGTCTTTTAATTGGAGGCTTGTATG
    138 GCAAAAGTACGTCGACGTGCACTGCCACGACAGTGACGACCAGAGCGTGAAGCTGTACAAGAACCAGATCGCC
```

By far the most common "sequence" is that of the all-`N` reads
you found in w4c.
The FastQC program, which you'll use in week 6,
reports such "overrepresented sequences" too.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: `sort`, `uniq`, and `paste`

a. The experiment has 2 time points and 3 treatments.
   Create a frequency table of the number of samples
   for each _combination_ of time point and treatment.
   Is the design balanced, i.e. does every combination have the same number of samples?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>
   Select both the time point and the treatment column with `cut`.
   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Select columns 2 and 3 with `cut -f 2,3`,
   and keep the rest of the w4c frequency table pipeline the same:

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 2,3 | sort | uniq -c
   ```
   ```bash-out
         4 10dpi   cathemerium
         4 10dpi   control
         4 10dpi   relictum
         3 24hpi   cathemerium
         3 24hpi   control
         4 24hpi   relictum
   ```

   Because `uniq` compares entire lines,
   it counts each distinct combination of time point and treatment.
   The design is not fully balanced:
   at 24hpi, there are only 3 samples for both the cathemerium and control treatments.
   </details>

b. A labmate wants to sort the GTF file by start position (column 4).
   They remove the header lines and then sort as follows:

   ```bash
   grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | sort -k4
   ```

   Without running it, can you spot two problems with this command?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   1. Without `n`, the start positions are sorted alphabetically,
      so that, e.g., `160196` would come before `2046`.
   2. The sequence ID (column 1) is ignored,
      so features from different chromosomes and scaffolds get mixed up.
      To sort by position _within_ each sequence, use `sort -k1,1 -k4,4n`.

   _(A minor third point: `-k4` means "from column 4 to the end of the line",_
   _rather than just column 4 as `-k4,4` would.)_

   You can see the second problem right away in the output,
   whose first lines come from three different scaffolds:

   ```bash
   grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | sort -k4 | head -n 3 | cut -f 1-5
   ```
   ```bash-out
   NW_026292908.1  Gnomon  CDS     10      11481
   NW_026292919.1  Gnomon  CDS     10      1167
   NW_026292909.1  Gnomon  CDS     10      1587
   ```
   </details>

c. `paste - - - -` is a safe way to put each FASTQ read on a single line.
   Would `paste - -` similarly be a safe way to put each sequence in `genome.fna`
   on a single line, next to its header? Why or why not?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   No: in FASTQ files, every record consists of exactly 4 lines,
   but in FASTA files, a sequence can be spread across any number of lines
   (recall exercise 2 in the [w4a slides](../week04/w4a_genomics-files.qmd)).
   In `genome.fna`, each line holds 80 bases,
   so `paste - -` would mostly paste one 80-base line next to the next one.
   </details>
:::

## `tr` to translate characters

### Substituting characters

The `tr` (**tr**anslate) command substitutes characters one-for-one:
the first character in its first argument is replaced by the first character
in its second argument, and so on.
For example, to replace every `a` by a `b`:

```bash
echo "aaaaccc" | tr 'a' 'b'
```
```bash-out
bbbbccc
```

Oddly enough, `tr` does not accept a file name as an argument:
it only reads from standard input.
So, to use it on a file, pipe the output of `cat` into `tr`.
For example, to turn the Tab-separated `metadata.tsv` into a comma-separated file,
replace each Tab (`\t`) by a comma:

```bash
cat metadata.tsv | tr '\t' ',' > metadata.csv
head -n 3 metadata.csv
```
```bash-out
sample_id,time,treatment
S82,10dpi,cathemerium
S75,10dpi,cathemerium
```

`tr` also understands **ranges** of characters.
This is handy because many genome FASTA files, including ours,
are "**soft-masked**": repetitive regions are written in lowercase letters.
For example, lines 12 and 13 of the genome FASTA file contain both:

```bash
head -n 13 genome.fna | tail -n 2
```
```bash-out
CCTAATTCATGGAGGTGAATAGAGCATACGTAAATACAAAACTCATGACATTAGCCTGTAAGGATTGTGTaattaatgca
aaaatattgaTAGAATGAAAGATGCAAGTCccaaaaattttaagtaaatgaATAGTAATCATAAAGATAActgatgatga
```

To convert everything to uppercase, translate the range `a-z` into `A-Z`:

```bash
head -n 13 genome.fna | tail -n 2 | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
```
```bash-out
CCTAATTCATGGAGGTGAATAGAGCATACGTAAATACAAAACTCATGACATTAGCCTGTAAGGATTGTGTAATTAATGCA
AAAATATTGATAGAATGAAAGATGCAAGTCCCAAAAATTTTAAGTAAATGAATAGTAATCATAAAGATAACTGATGATGA
```

### Reverse complementing a sequence

Combined with `rev`, which reverses each line,
`tr` can create the **reverse complement** of a DNA sequence:
`rev` takes care of the "reverse" part, and `tr` of the "complement" part
by swapping `A` with `T` and `C` with `G`:

```bash
echo "ATGCCGTA" | rev | tr 'ACGT' 'TGCA'
```
```bash-out
TACGGCAT
```

### Deleting and "squeezing" characters

- The **`-d`** option **deletes** characters.
  For example, by deleting all newlines (`\n`) from the sequence lines of the genome FASTA,
  you can count the total number of bases in the genome assembly
  (this takes a few seconds):

  ```bash
  grep -v '^>' genome.fna | tr -d '\n' | wc -c
  ```
  ```bash-out
  566354144
  ```

  So, the _Culex pipiens_ genome assembly is about 566 million bases (566 Mb) long.

- The **`-s`** option "**squeezes**" runs of the same character into one.
  For example, to turn a variable number of spaces into a single space:

  ```bash
  echo "a     b   c" | tr -s ' '
  ```
  ```bash-out
  a b c
  ```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: `tr`

a. A labmate wants to rename the `control` treatment to `mock` in the metadata file,
   and runs the command below.
   What do you think the output will look like?
   Run the command to check.

   ```bash
   cat metadata.tsv | tr 'control' 'mock'
   ```

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   The output is mangled, also outside of the `control` lines:

   ```bash-out
   sampke_id       kime    kkeakmeck
   S82     10dpi   makhemekium
   S75     10dpi   makhemekium
   [...]
   S78     10dpi   mkckkkk
   S84     10dpi   mkckkkk
   [...]
   ```

   `tr` translates individual _characters_, not words:
   every `c` became an `m`, every `n` a `c`, and so on, anywhere in the file.
   Because the second argument is shorter than the first,
   the remaining characters (`t`, `r`, `o`, and `l`) all became its last character, `k`.

   To replace a word, use `sed`, which is covered below.
   </details>

b. Use `tr` to calculate which percentage of the genome assembly is soft-masked
   (i.e., written in lowercase).

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>
   Combine `-d` with the **`-c`** option, which takes the complement of the
   (first) set of characters: e.g., `tr -cd 'xyz'` deletes everything _except_
   `x`, `y`, and `z`.
   Then compare with the total of 566,354,144 bases.
   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Delete everything except lowercase bases, and count the remaining characters:

   ```bash
   grep -v '^>' genome.fna | tr -cd 'acgtn' | wc -c
   ```
   ```bash-out
   315245493
   ```

   315,245,493 / 566,354,144 = 0.56, so **56%** of the assembly is soft-masked.
   Large fractions of many genomes, including those of mosquitoes,
   consist of repetitive DNA such as transposable elements.

   _(The `grep -v '^>'` step is needed because the header lines contain lowercase letters too.)_
   </details>

c. A labmate wants the reverse complement of the entire genome, and runs:

   ```bash
   rev genome.fna | tr 'ACGT' 'TGCA' > genome_revcomp.fna
   ```

   Without running it, can you name at least two problems with this command?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   1. `rev` reverses each _line_ separately,
      but leaves the order of the lines unchanged.
      Because the sequences are spread across many lines,
      they are therefore not properly reversed.
   2. The header lines are also reversed and "complemented":
      e.g., the first header would end in `[...] sneipip xeluG 1.739860_GN>`.
   3. Lowercase (soft-masked) bases are not complemented,
      since `tr` is case-sensitive.

   This is a task for a dedicated bioinformatics tool.
   </details>
:::

## `awk` for tabular data processing

`awk` is a small programming language in its own right,
which is especially good at quickly processing tabular data.
For example, it can select rows based on the values in specific columns,
reorder columns, or do calculations.
To understand `awk`, you need to know about two core concepts:
**records and fields**, and **pattern-action pairs**.

### Records and fields

`awk` processes its input one **record** at a time,
and by default, each line is one record.
Within a record, each column is a **field**.
The entire record is available as `$0`, and the fields as
`$1` (first column), `$2` (second column), and so on.

An `awk` command is placed between single quotes,
and actions go between curly braces `{ }`.
For example, to print columns 3 and 1 of the metadata file:

```bash
awk '{ print $3, $1 }' metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
treatment sample_id
cathemerium S82
cathemerium S75
```

This already goes beyond `cut`, which can't change the order of columns.
Note how the comma `,` between the columns made `awk` separate them with a space.
Without the comma, the columns are pasted together,
and to separate them with a Tab, you can add a `"\t"`:

```bash
awk '{ print $3 $1 }' metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
treatmentsample_id
cathemeriumS82
cathemeriumS75
```

```bash
awk '{ print $3 "\t" $1 }' metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
treatment       sample_id
cathemerium     S82
cathemerium     S75
```

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Set the column delimiter with `-F '\t'` for TSV files

By default, `awk` splits fields on _any_ whitespace: Tabs as well as spaces.
That works for the metadata file, which contains no spaces,
but not for the GTF file, whose ninth column contains spaces.
See what happens when you try to print column 9 of a GTF line:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | head -n 1 | awk '{ print $9 }'
```
```bash-out
gene_id
```

The built-in variable `NF` (**n**umber of **f**ields) shows that `awk`
split this line into 24 fields, rather than the 9 columns of a GTF file:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | head -n 1 | awk '{ print NF }'
```
```bash-out
24
```

With **`-F '\t'`**, you tell `awk` to only split fields on Tabs:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | head -n 1 | awk -F '\t' '{ print NF }'
```
```bash-out
9
```

To be safe, always use `-F '\t'` with Tab-separated files.
:::

### Pattern-action pairs

The general syntax of an `awk` command is **`awk 'pattern { action }' file`**, where:

- The **pattern** is a condition that is tested for each record.
- The **action** is performed for each record for which the pattern is true.

Either of the two can be omitted:

- Omit the pattern, like in the examples above, and the action is performed for _every_ record.
- Omit the action, and every record that matches the pattern is printed in full.

#### Patterns

Patterns are often comparisons, such as `$3 == "control"`
(column 3 equals "control"; note the double `==` and the quotes around the text).
Patterns can also be combined, for example with `&&` ("and").
To print all infected (i.e., non-control) samples from the 24hpi time point:

```bash
awk '$2 == "24hpi" && $3 != "control"' metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
S64     24hpi   cathemerium
S67     24hpi   cathemerium
S70     24hpi   cathemerium
S71     24hpi   relictum
S74     24hpi   relictum
S65     24hpi   relictum
S68     24hpi   relictum
```

Here are the most important comparison and logical operators:

| Operator    | Meaning
|-------------|-------------|
| `a == b`    | `a` is equal to `b`
| `a != b`    | `a` is not equal to `b`
| `a < b` / `a > b` | `a` is less than / greater than `b`
| `a <= b` / `a >= b` | `a` is less than or equal to / greater than or equal to `b`
| `a ~ /b/`   | `a` matches regular expression `b`
| `a !~ /b/`  | `a` does not match regular expression `b`
| `a && b`    | `a` **and** `b`
| `a` <code>&#124;&#124;</code> `b` | `a` **or** `b`
| `!a`        | **not** `a`

: {.striped .hover}

As the `~` operator shows, `awk` can also use regular expressions,
which go between forward slashes.
For example, `$1 ~ /^NW_/` would select features on the unplaced scaffolds.

You can also **calculate** in patterns.
For example, the length of a GTF feature is its end position (column 5)
minus its start position (column 4), plus 1^[
The plus 1 is needed because GTF coordinates are "1-based and inclusive":
a feature with start and end position 2046 is 1 base long.
Watch out: in other formats, like BED, this is not the case.].
So, to print all genes longer than 1 Mb (1,000,000 bases):

```bash
awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene" && $5 - $4 + 1 > 1000000' annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
NC_068939.1     Gnomon  gene    10362825        11542514        .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120432606"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120432606"; description "RNA-binding protein Musashi homolog Rbp6"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120432606"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
```

Only one gene, on chromosome 3, is that long.

#### Actions

Patterns and actions can of course be combined.
For example, to print the sequence ID, start, end, and length of each gene:

```bash
awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene" { print $1, $4, $5, $5 - $4 + 1 }' annot.gtf | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1 2046 110808 108763
NC_068937.1 48457 50554 2098
NC_068937.1 76295 82374 6080
```

### `BEGIN` and `END`

Two special patterns are **`BEGIN`** and **`END`**,
whose actions are performed once:
before the first record and after the last record, respectively.

`BEGIN` is often used to set options.
For example, setting the variable `OFS` (**o**utput **f**ield **s**eparator)
to a Tab makes the commas in `print` produce Tabs instead of spaces:

```bash
awk -F '\t' 'BEGIN { OFS = "\t" } $3 == "gene" { print $1, $4, $5, $5 - $4 + 1 }' annot.gtf | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     2046    110808  108763
NC_068937.1     48457   50554   2098
NC_068937.1     76295   82374   6080
```

`END` is useful for printing a summary after processing all records.
For example, to compute the mean gene length,
add up the lengths of all genes in a variable `sum`,
count the genes in a variable `n`,
and divide the two at the end:

```bash
awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene" { sum += $5 - $4 + 1; n++ } END { print sum / n }' annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
18961.9
```

In this command:

- `sum += x` is shorthand for `sum = sum + x`, and `n++` for `n = n + 1`.
- Two statements within one action are separated by a semicolon `;`.
- You don't need to create (initialize) `sum` and `n` beforehand:
  `awk` variables start out as 0.

### Processing FASTQ files with `awk`

The built-in variable **`NR`** holds the current record (line) number.
This is very handy for FASTQ files, where the sequence is always on
the 2nd line of each 4-line record:
the lines for which `NR % 4 == 2` (the remainder after dividing the line number by 4 is 2).
Combined with the `length()` function,
this gives you the length of every read --- and then, a frequency table of read lengths:

```bash
zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 { print length($0) }' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5
```
```bash-out
 303297 74
 123453 73
  32678 35
  28617 72
   8483 71
```

Most reads are 72--74 bases long,
but 32,678 reads are only 35 bases long:
the all-`N` reads you saw in w4c and in the `paste` section above.

### `awk` reference tables

Some useful built-in variables:

| Variable  | Meaning
|-----------|------------|
| `$0`      | The entire record (by default, a line)
| `$1`, `$2`, ... | The first, second, ... field (by default, a column)
| `NR`      | **N**umber of the current **r**ecord (in `END`: total number of records)
| `NF`      | **N**umber of **f**ields in the current record
| `FS`      | Input **f**ield **s**eparator (set with `-F`; default: any whitespace)
| `OFS`     | **O**utput **f**ield **s**eparator (default: a space)

: {.striped .hover}

Some useful functions and statements:

| Function / statement | Meaning
|----------------------|--------------------------------|
| `length(s)`          | Number of characters in `s` (`length()` alone: in the whole record)
| `tolower(s)` / `toupper(s)` | `s` converted to lowercase / uppercase
| `substr(s, start, n)` | The part of `s` that starts at position `start` and is `n` characters long
| `split(s, arr, sep)` | Splits `s` into pieces on `sep`, and stores the pieces in array `arr`
| `sub(regex, repl, s)` | Replaces the first match of `regex` in `s` by `repl`
| `gsub(regex, repl, s)` | Replaces every match of `regex` in `s` by `repl`
| `next`               | Skips to the next record, without considering any remaining pattern-action pairs
| `exit`               | Stops processing records (any `END` action is still performed)

: {.striped .hover}

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 4: `awk`

a. A classmate wants to print the control samples, but makes a small typo:

   ```bash
   awk '$3 = "control"' metadata.tsv
   ```

   What do you think this will print? Run the command to check.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   It prints _every_ line, with the third column replaced by `control`
   (and with spaces instead of Tabs between the columns):

   ```bash-out
   sample_id time control
   S82 10dpi control
   S75 10dpi control
   [...]
   ```

   A single `=` doesn't compare but _assigns_ a value:
   it sets column 3 to `control` for every line.
   Furthermore, the result of that assignment, the text `control`, counts as "true",
   so every line is printed.
   When `awk` changes a field, it rebuilds the line using `OFS`, which is a space by default.

   With `==`, the command works as intended:

   ```bash
   awk '$3 == "control"' metadata.tsv
   ```
   </details>

b. Compute the mean length of exons.
   Why do you think it is so much shorter than the mean gene length of nearly 19,000 bases?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Change the pattern from `"gene"` to `"exon"`:

   ```bash
   awk -F '\t' '$3 == "exon" { sum += $5 - $4 + 1; n++ } END { print sum / n }' annot.gtf
   ```
   ```bash-out
   542.133
   ```

   Exons are only about 540 bases long on average,
   because most genes consist of multiple exons separated by introns,
   which are often much longer than the exons.
   The length of a gene spans all of its exons _and_ introns.
   </details>

c. Remove all reads shorter than 50 bases from `S63_R1.fastq.gz`,
   and save the remaining reads in a new FASTQ file `S63_R1_filtered.fastq`.
   How many reads are left?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>
   Put each read on one line with `paste`, filter with `awk`,
   and then turn each line back into a 4-line FASTQ record with `tr`.
   (The `length()` function can also take a specific field, like `length($2)`.)
   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   After `paste - - - -`, the sequence is in column 2,
   so keep only lines with `length($2) >= 50`.
   Then, replace the Tabs that `paste` inserted by newlines:

   ```bash
   zcat S63_R1.fastq.gz |
       paste - - - - |
       awk -F '\t' 'length($2) >= 50' |
       tr '\t' '\n' > S63_R1_filtered.fastq
   ```

   _(A line that ends with a pipe `|` continues on the next line,_
   _which makes long pipelines easier to read.)_

   Count the reads by dividing the number of lines by 4:

   ```bash
   wc -l S63_R1_filtered.fastq
   ```
   ```bash-out
   1869040 S63_R1_filtered.fastq
   ```

   1,869,040 / 4 = 467,260 reads are left,
   so 32,740 reads were shorter than 50 bases.

   _(In practice, you would use a dedicated read-trimming program for this,_
   _which can filter reads by length and quality in one go.)_
   </details>
:::

## `sed` to find and replace

### Substitution with `s/pattern/replacement/`

`sed` (**s**tream **ed**itor) is most often used to **find and replace** text,
using the syntax **`s/pattern/replacement/`**, where `s` stands for "substitute".
Unlike `tr`, `sed` replaces whole patterns rather than single characters.
So, here is how you _can_ rename the `control` treatment to `mock`
(recall Exercise 3a):

```bash
sed 's/control/mock/' metadata.tsv | head -n 8 | tail -n 4
```
```bash-out
S83     10dpi   cathemerium
S78     10dpi   mock
S84     10dpi   mock
S77     10dpi   mock
```

The pattern is a regular expression,
and by default, `sed` only replaces the **first match on each line**.
To replace all matches, add the **`g`** ("global") modifier at the end:

```bash
echo "AAACCCAAA" | sed 's/A/T/'
```
```bash-out
TAACCCAAA
```

```bash
echo "AAACCCAAA" | sed 's/A/T/g'
```
```bash-out
TTTCCCTTT
```

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Saving the output of `sed`

Like the other commands on this page,
`sed` does not change the input file, but prints its output to the screen.
To save the output, redirect it to a _new_ file
(recall from w4c that you should never redirect to the input file itself):

```bash
sed 's/control/mock/' metadata.tsv > metadata_mock.tsv
```

`sed` also has an **`-i`** option to edit a file **in place**,
e.g. `sed -i 's/control/mock/' metadata.tsv`.
This is convenient, but be careful: there is no undo,
so make sure your command works before adding `-i`.
:::

### Selecting lines with addresses

By default, `sed` operates on every line.
You can restrict it to certain lines by putting an "**address**" in front of the command:
either a line number or range of line numbers, or a regular expression between slashes.
For example, many tools use only the first "word" of a FASTA header as the sequence ID,
and long headers can be a nuisance.
To remove everything from the first space onwards, but only on header lines:

```bash
sed '/^>/ s/ .*//' genome.fna | grep '^>' | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
>NC_068937.1
>NC_068938.1
>NC_068939.1
```

Besides `s`, two other handy `sed` commands are `d` (**d**elete) and `p` (**p**rint):

- `sed '/^#/d' annot.gtf` deletes all lines starting with `#`,
  i.e. it does the same as `grep -v '^#' annot.gtf`.
- `sed '1d' metadata.tsv` deletes the first line,
  i.e. it does the same as `tail -n +2 metadata.tsv`.
- `sed -n '12,13p' genome.fna` prints lines 12 to 13.
  The `-n` option turns off `sed`'s default printing of every line,
  so only the lines selected with `p` are printed.

### Using a different delimiter

The `/` in `s/pattern/replacement/` can be replaced by (almost) any other character.
This is useful when the pattern or replacement contains slashes, like file paths.
For example, to remove the dirs from a list of file paths
(the `.*/` greedily matches everything up to and including the _last_ `/`):

```bash
ls ../../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz | sed 's#.*/##' | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
S63_R1.fastq.gz
S63_R2.fastq.gz
S64_R1.fastq.gz
```

To apply multiple substitutions in one `sed` command, put **`-e`** before each one.
For example, to also remove the read direction and extension,
and get a list of sample IDs:

```bash
ls ../../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz | sed -e 's#.*/##' -e 's/_R[12]\.fastq\.gz$//' | sort -u | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
S63
S64
S65
```

### Capture groups and backreferences

A powerful regex feature is that you can **capture** parts of a match by putting
them in parentheses `( )`,
and then **recall** them in the replacement with `\1` (the first group),
`\2` (the second group), and so on.
(Use `sed -E`, so that the parentheses don't need backslashes.)

For example, genomic regions are often written as `<seqID>:<start>-<end>`.
To turn such a region into three Tab-separated columns:

```bash
echo "NC_068937.1:2046-110808" | sed -E 's/^([^:]+):([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)$/\1\t\2\t\3/'
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     2046    110808
```

Here, `([^:]+)` captures everything up to the colon,
and each `([0-9]+)` captures a number.

Capture groups are also a way to extract information from a line.
For example, to extract the gene ID from the GTF's gene lines,
match the _entire_ line,
and replace it by just the captured ID:

```bash
awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene"' annot.gtf | sed -E 's/.*gene_id "([^"]+)".*/\1/' | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
LOC120427725
LOC120427726
LOC128092783
```

Let's try the same with the transcript IDs, on all lines of the GTF file:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | sed -E 's/.*transcript_id "([^"]+)".*/\1/' | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  gene    2046    110808  .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; description "homeotic protein deformed"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120427725"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
XM_052707445.1
XM_052707445.1
```

What went wrong in the first line?
Gene lines have an empty transcript ID (`transcript_id ""`),
which doesn't match `[^"]+` (one or more non-quote characters).
And when the pattern doesn't match, `sed` simply prints the line unchanged.

The solution is to combine the `-n` option with the `p` modifier,
which prints a line only if a substitution was made:

```bash
grep -v '^#' annot.gtf | sed -E -n 's/.*transcript_id "([^"]+)".*/\1/p' | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
XM_052707445.1
XM_052707445.1
XM_052707445.1
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 5: `sed`

a. Above, `sed 's#.*/##'` removed the dirs from a file path.
   What do you think the command below will print instead? Run it to check.

   ```bash
   echo "../../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz" | sed 's#/.*##'
   ```

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```bash-out
   ..
   ```

   The pattern `/.*` matches the _first_ `/` and everything after it,
   so only the first `..` is left.
   </details>

b. Create a version of the metadata file in which the `time` column holds
   the number of hours post-infection:
   `240` instead of `10dpi`, and `24` instead of `24hpi`.
   Also rename the column header from `time` to `time_h`
   --- make sure that only the header is affected.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>
   Use `-e` for multiple substitutions,
   and an address to restrict the header change to line 1.
   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```bash
   sed -e '1s/time/time_h/' -e 's/10dpi/240/' -e 's/24hpi/24/' metadata.tsv > metadata_hours.tsv
   head -n 3 metadata_hours.tsv
   ```
   ```bash-out
   sample_id       time_h  treatment
   S82     240     cathemerium
   S75     240     cathemerium
   ```

   In this case, `s/time/time_h/` without the `1` address would have worked too,
   because no other line contains `time`.
   But with the address, you can be sure that only the header line is changed.
   </details>

c. Do the reverse of the `sed` capture group example above:
   for each gene in the GTF file, print its region in the format
   `<seqID>:<start>-<end>`, e.g. `NC_068937.1:2046-110808`.
   Can you think of a way to do this with `awk` instead?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   With `sed`, first select the gene lines and the relevant columns,
   and then capture and rearrange the three columns:

   ```bash
   awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene"' annot.gtf | cut -f 1,4,5 |
       sed -E 's/^([^\t]+)\t([0-9]+)\t([0-9]+)$/\1:\2-\3/' | head -n 3
   ```
   ```bash-out
   NC_068937.1:2046-110808
   NC_068937.1:48457-50554
   NC_068937.1:76295-82374
   ```

   With `awk`, this is a lot simpler:
   print the columns separated by the desired text (between quotes):

   ```bash
   awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene" { print $1 ":" $4 "-" $5 }' annot.gtf | head -n 3
   ```

   As you can see, there is often more than one way to do something with these tools.
   </details>
:::

## Putting it together: genes per chromosome

As a final example, let's combine several of the tools on this page
to answer a biological question:
**how gene-dense is each chromosome?**
To compute the number of genes per million bases (Mb) for each sequence,
you'll need information from two files:
sequence lengths from the genome FASTA, and gene counts from the GTF.
You'll then merge these with a new command, `join`.

### Step 1: Sequence lengths from the FASTA file

Computing the length of each sequence in a FASTA file takes a slightly more
complex `awk` command,
because each sequence is spread across many lines:

```bash
awk '/^>/ { if (id) print id "\t" len; id = substr($1, 2); len = 0; next }
     { len += length($0) }
     END { print id "\t" len }' genome.fna | sort -k1,1 > seq_lengths.tsv
```

Here is what this does:

- For **header lines** (pattern `/^>/`):
  - If this isn't the first header, print the ID and length of the _previous_ sequence.
  - Store the new sequence ID: the first field without the `>`
    (`substr($1, 2)` takes everything from the 2nd character onwards).
  - Reset the length to 0, and skip to the next line (`next`).
- For **sequence lines** (no pattern, but header lines never get here because of `next`):
  add the number of bases on the line to the length.
- At the **end**, print the ID and length of the last sequence,
  which hasn't been printed yet.
- Finally, sort by sequence ID, which `join` will need.

```bash
head -n 4 seq_lengths.tsv
```
```bash-out
NC_015079.1     14856
NC_068937.1     139153999
NC_068938.1     224097512
NC_068939.1     186194774
```

### Step 2: Gene counts from the GTF file

To count the genes on each sequence,
make a frequency table of column 1 for the gene lines.
Then, swap the two columns of `uniq -c`'s output with `awk`,
so that the sequence ID comes first, as in the other file:

```bash
awk -F '\t' '$3 == "gene"' annot.gtf | cut -f 1 | sort | uniq -c |
    awk '{ print $2 "\t" $1 }' > gene_counts.tsv

head -n 4 gene_counts.tsv
```
```bash-out
NC_015079.1     13
NC_068937.1     5173
NC_068938.1     7532
NC_068939.1     6248
```

### Step 3: Merging the two files with `join`

`join` merges two files based on a shared column ---
by default, the first column of each file.
For every sequence ID that occurs in both files,
it prints the ID followed by the remaining columns of both files:

```bash
join seq_lengths.tsv gene_counts.tsv | head -n 4
```
```bash-out
NC_015079.1 14856 13
NC_068937.1 139153999 5173
NC_068938.1 224097512 7532
NC_068939.1 186194774 6248
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
`join` requires both files to be **sorted** on the join column.
If they aren't, it will miss matches (usually, but not always, with a warning).
:::

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>The joined output has fewer lines than `seq_lengths.tsv`. Which sequences are missing, and why?</summary>

`join` only prints lines whose ID occurs in _both_ files (this is called an "inner join").
Sequences without any annotated genes don't occur in `gene_counts.tsv`,
so they're left out.
To also keep the lines that only occur in the first file, use `join -a 1`.
</details>

### Step 4: Computing gene density

Finally, use `awk` to divide the number of genes (column 3)
by the length in Mb (column 2 divided by 1,000,000),
and only keep the sequences with `NC` IDs:

```bash
join seq_lengths.tsv gene_counts.tsv |
    awk '{ print $1, $2, $3, $3 / ($2 / 1000000) }' |
    grep '^NC'
```
```bash-out
NC_015079.1 14856 13 875.067
NC_068937.1 139153999 5173 37.1746
NC_068938.1 224097512 7532 33.6104
NC_068939.1 186194774 6248 33.5563
```

So, the three chromosomes have a similar gene density of about 34--37 genes per Mb.
The mitochondrial genome (`NC_015079.1`) is far more gene-dense:
its 13 genes are packed into fewer than 15,000 bases.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
For more complex merges of tables, R is a better tool:
its _dplyr_ package, which you'll learn about in week 13,
has a set of flexible `join` functions.
:::

## Wrap-up: which tool when?

| Task                                            | Tool(s)
|-------------------------------------------------|---------------------------
| Find lines that contain a (regex) pattern       | `grep`
| Extract the matching part of lines              | `grep -o`, or `sed -E` with capture groups
| Select columns                                  | `cut`; `awk` to also reorder them
| Select rows based on the values in a column     | `awk`
| Calculate with values in columns                | `awk`
| Replace text                                    | `sed`; `tr` for single characters
| Count or summarize values                       | `sort` and `uniq -c`
| Merge two tables                                | `join`

: {.striped .hover}

These tools shine for quick, one-off questions about (large) files,
and for small processing steps in shell scripts.
But when a pipeline gets long or hard to read,
it's often better to switch to:

- **R or Python**, for more complex data wrangling, statistics, and plotting
  (you'll start learning R in week 12).
- **Dedicated bioinformatics tools**, for format-specific tasks like
  filtering or reverse complementing reads and sequences.
  Such tools handle the details of file formats
  (like multi-line FASTA sequences, or soft-masked bases) for you.

Finally, now that you're done with this page,
remove the large genome FASTA file:

```bash
rm genome.fna
```

<br>
